title: Medical Needs Kit
description: Use this list if anyone in your household depends on medicines, medical devices, or special care, so their needs are covered when power, pharmacies, or transport fail.

sources.title: FDA Offers Tips About Medical Devices and Natural Disasters
Information Regarding Insulin Storage and Switching Between Products in an Emergency
Safe Drug Use After a Natural Disaster

items.text: Written list for each person: medicines with strength and schedule, allergies, conditions, doctors, pharmacy, and device model numbers - copies in each go-bag and a photo on your phone
At least a 7-14 day reserve of every daily prescription, built legally with your doctor, pharmacist, and insurer, and rotated oldest-first
Device power plan: battery run times, spare charged batteries, chargers, and whether it can run on a car outlet, power station, or generator
Tell your electric utility and fire department if someone relies on powered medical equipment
Cooler and frozen gel packs for refrigerated medicines - keep them from touching ice, since freezing ruins insulin
Write each refrigerated medicine's room-temperature limit from its label (many insulins: up to 28 days at 59-86 F / 15-30 C)
Backup oxygen cylinders sized for your flow rate, stored upright and secured, with no flames or smoking nearby
Backup supplies for pumps: pens or syringes and a written pump-failure plan from your clinician
Glucose tablets, testing supplies, and spare inhalers or epinephrine auto-injectors as needed
Plan for medicines you must not stop suddenly (seizure, heart, steroid, psychiatric) - know who to call for an emergency refill
Support network of at least three people per place (home, work, school) who know how to help and operate equipment
Accessible transportation and evacuation plan, including how to get down stairs if elevators stop
Ask officials about early evacuation if a life depends on a device and long power loss is expected
Extra glasses, hearing aids and batteries, catheters, ostomy and incontinence supplies
Medical alert bracelet or wallet card
Food for special diets for at least 3 days, and extra water if the doctor advises
Alerts in a usable form: text alerts, a strobe or vibrating weather radio, or large-print plans
Copies of insurance cards, prescriptions, and key medical records in a waterproof bag
Label equipment with the owner's name and phone number
Service animal supplies: food, tags, vaccination proof, and vet contacts
Ask home health, dialysis, and oxygen providers for their disaster and backup plans
Throw out medicines that touched floodwater unless one is life-saving, has no replacement, and looks normal - replace it as soon as you can
After an outage, check device settings did not reset, and never plug in a wet device
